title: Who Pays for Missing Selenium? An Actor-Resolved Cost Cascade from Soil to Human Health and the Break-Even Case for Selenium-Enriched Fertilisation in Austria
content: Selenium (Se) is essential for animals and humans but not for higher plants. The farmer may therefore gain nothing from correcting a Se-poor soil, while potential costs arise further down the food chain. An ex-ante cost model for Austria follows the deficit from soil to crop, feed, animal and human and assigns costs by actor (EUR 2025). Without a yield response, Se fertilisation at 10 g ha−1 (EUR 6.84 ha−1) gives the arable producer no return; at the Austrian wheat price, a yield gain of 41 kg ha−1 would make it profitable. Livestock producers add Se to feed at EUR 0.005–0.04 per fattening pig, without effect on cereal foods. Austrian field trials indicate about 4.5 µg of additional daily intake per person from domestic wheat and rye. Treating all 741,200 ha of cereals would cost EUR 5.6 million per year (EUR 0.60 per inhabitant) and would pay for itself if it avoided 0.7–3.7% of the cost of hypothyroidism alone. A co-limitation framework shows where low Se can limit the benefit of iodine, iron, copper, zinc, manganese and vitamin E.
